summary: This standards-track document extends OSPF Traffic Engineering to advertise link availability for links whose bandwidth varies in discrete steps, such as microwave links. Operators typically use availability when planning networks, and this extension lets routers carry that information in their link-state advertisements. Path computation can then take it into account.

eli5.summary: A bridge that only works some of the time is less reliable than one that always works. This lets routers say how often each road is open so they can pick dependable ones.

how does ospf-te handle microwave links
subtitle: How OSPF-TE routers advertise how much bandwidth a variable-rate link can guarantee at each availability level.

tldr.problem: Links such as microwave and copper can change their bandwidth in discrete steps, so a router needs to know how much bandwidth each link can guarantee at a given availability before routing an LSP over it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8330 defines an Availability SCSI-TLV, carried in OSPF-TE advertisements, that pairs an availability level with an LSP bandwidth. A link can advertise several pairs.
tldr.outcome: Routers and path computation elements get the data they need to pick paths, though how availability is measured and used is left to other documents.

facts.label: Switching types added
facts.value: 5 (PSC with GSCSI support), 52 (L2SC with GSCSI support)

today: RFC 8330 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the signaling extension to a separate document and expects technology-specific documents to describe specific uses.

sections.title: Links with Variable Bandwidth
sections.content:
Some data-plane technologies, such as microwave and copper, can change their maximum physical bandwidth among a set of known discrete values. Operators describe such links with availability: the proportion of operating time that the requested bandwidth is ensured.

Before setting up a Label Switched Path (LSP) over these links, nodes need availability information to check the bandwidth before reserving it. The availability is determined by the operator and statically configured, usually from the needs of the services the LSP will carry. Voice usually needs "five nines", while non-real-time services may do well with four or three nines. Because service types differ, a link may need several <availability, bandwidth> pairs.
sections.eli5: A road that sometimes floods can carry lots of cars on sunny days and few on rainy days. Delivery companies want to know how many trucks fit in each kind of weather.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
A node with links of variable discrete bandwidth should include an <availability, bandwidth> list in its OSPF-TE LSA messages. The list maps the link's nominal bandwidth to its availability level. The information is flooded through the network so nodes, or a PCE, can use it in path calculation, and the computed path can then be provisioned by signaling.

The RFC defines a new type of Generalized SCSI-TLV (Switching Capability-Specific Information), the Availability SCSI-TLV. It only distributes the information. Measuring availability and using it for route computation are outside its scope, and technology-specific documents are expected to reference it.
sections.eli5: Each router shouts out a small table: at this much reliability, I can carry this much traffic. Every other router hears it and can plan routes.

sections.title: The Availability SCSI-TLV
sections.content:
The Generalized SCSI is defined in RFC 8258. The Availability SCSI-TLV can be included one or more times. Its fields are:

  • Type: 0x000A, 16 bits.
  • Length: 2 octets (16 bits).
  • Availability level: 32 bits, a binary32 floating-point number from IEEE 754-2008, sent in network order. It gives the decimal availability guarantee of the Switching Capability in the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor. The value MUST be less than 1, and is usually 0.99, 0.999, 0.9999 or 0.99999.
  • LSP Bandwidth at Availability level n: 32 bits, also an IEEE floating-point number in network order, in bytes per second.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny form with three boxes: what kind of note this is, how reliable the link is, and how much traffic it can carry at that reliability.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
An Interface Switching Capability Descriptor (ISCD) lets routing protocols such as OSPF carry technology-specific data (RFC 4203). A node advertising an interface whose Switching Capability supports variable discrete bandwidth SHOULD include one or more Availability SCSI-TLVs in its OSPF-TE LSAs.

The TLV MUST NOT be sent in ISCDs with Switching Capability values that have not been defined to support it, because non-supporting nodes would see such an ISCD or LSA as malformed. If the TLV is absent from an ISCD whose Switching Capability does support it, the link is read as a fixed-bandwidth link with the highest availability value.

Only one TLV per availability level SHOULD be sent. If several are present, the one with the lowest bandwidth value SHALL be processed. A TLV with an invalid value, such as a level larger than 1, is ignored.
sections.eli5: Only use the form on roads that know about it. If a road gives two different numbers for the same reliability, believe the smaller one. Throw away forms with silly numbers.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The document specifies contents of Opaque LSAs in OSPFv2, and tampering with GMPLS-TE LSAs may affect TE computations. It points to the protections suggested by RFC 3630, such as the approach in RFC 2154, and to the OSPF security analysis in RFC 6863. Any new mechanism that protects Opaque LSAs will automatically protect this extension. Broader threats are covered in RFC 5920.

IANA registered the Availability TLV as type 0x000A in the "Generalized SCSI TLV Types" registry, for switching types 5 and 52. It also registered two switching types: 5, "PSC with GSCSI support", and 52, "L2SC with GSCSI support".
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks a fake note into the shared table, routers could pick bad roads. So the notes should be protected the same way other routing notes are.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length field, given as 2 octets (16 bits).

fields.name: Availability level
fields.desc: Binary32 floating-point availability guarantee; MUST be less than 1.

fields.name: LSP Bandwidth at Availability level n
fields.desc: Floating-point LSP bandwidth for that level, in bytes per second.
